newsitem.title: UK: Italy becomes first country to raise debt in euros.
newsitem.headline: Italy becomes first country to raise debt in euros.

text.p: Italy successfully raised euro-denominated funds in international markets on Tuesday, becoming the first sovereign to borrow in the planned single European currency.

"The issue has been oversubscribed by investors across Europe...which indicates the increasing desire for investors to prepare themselves for EMU," said SBC Warburg, joint arranger of the offering with Paribas, in a statement.
Italy raised one billion euros through a seven-year Eurobond priced to yield 0.18 percentage point over an outstanding Ecu bond issued by France.

Until the euro is introduced at the third stage of European Economic and Monetary Union, trading in the bond will be settled in Ecu, the new currency's predecessor. So the bond totals one billion Ecu ($1.15 billion).
Italy is keen to be among the nations adopting the euro in the first wave of single currency participants, scheduled for January 1, 1999.
But financial markets have long held nagging doubts about Italy's chances of meeting the necessary qualifying criteria.

"The truly pan-European bid confirms that even though there has been noise of a possible delay to EMU, confidence still remains high EMU will occur. So investors want large liquid benchmark transactions," a spokesman for Paribas said.
An SBC Warburg syndicate manager said: "It's gone extremely well. We had a very successful pre-marketing session on Monday."
Dealers said the bond had performed very strongly after pricing because it was a must-have' issue for Ecu funds.
Late in the morning the yield spread had tightened to 0.15 percentage point on the buy side, a significant improvement for such a large, relatively long-dated Euromarket transaction.
Demand was such that banks involved in the bond said they had found themselves short of paper. "We've been through the broker looking to buy a few bonds," said one new issues manager.
SBC Warburg expected the deal would continue to outperform when retail investors got involved in the next week or two.
Other countries already have debt which may ultimately be repaid in euros after EMU, but only because of clauses in individual bond's terms.
Austria and Portugal earlier this year both made French franc bond issues whose terms and conditions contain language allowing for redenomination in euros.
Several quasi-state and corporate borrowers have also issued redenominatable bonds in the three core-EMU currencies, French franc, guilder and mark.
Many countries have outstanding Ecu bonds dating back to the late 1980s which will also be redenominated after EMU.
The European Investment Bank launched the first euro Eurobond in January this year.
